title: The arc measured, and the smallest criminal
summary: Mean, median, mode and range worked on your own four seasons of logs, the dawn thermometer and the crossing pace pages, gaps and all, and the question of which middle tells the truth. Then sprint 3's one new tool: if a claim ever fails there is a smallest failure, so arrest it, squeeze a smaller accomplice out of it, and the crime never happened. The month 3 monster goes up on the home card.
materials: the dawn temperature log and the field journal, gaps and all
the app open at its own counts for the four seasons
the pace pages from the half crossing and the first full crossing
jumbo chalk and a driveway for the line of stones
a coat hanger, two paper cups, string and twelve matching coins for the monster
one chocolate bar, optional and not compulsory

problems.prompt: Suppose all four seasons ran their full twelve weeks with all three tracks going: Build sixty minutes, Think seventy-five, Speak forty-five. About how many minutes of quests is that altogether?
explanation: One week of all three tracks is 60 plus 75 plus 45, which is 180 minutes.
Twelve weeks of that is about 2,200 minutes, and there are four seasons.
Round it: about 9,000 minutes, or about 150 hours.
problems.useAgain: when you want the size of something you have been doing in small pieces for a long time.
hints: Work out one whole week before you touch the twelve or the four.
Add the three track lengths first, then multiply twice.
problems.socraticHint: Would you have guessed higher or lower than that before you worked it out?

variant.prompt: Suppose you count only the Think track, seventy-five minutes a week, over the same four full seasons. About how many minutes is that?

problems.prompt: Your generator writes one test case: 100,000 whole numbers, one per line, each up to six digits long. About how big is that file?
explanation: One line is six digits plus the line ending, so call it 7 characters.
A hundred thousand of those is about 700,000 characters, and a character is about a byte.
That is about 700 kilobytes, nowhere near the thousand kilobytes a megabyte needs.
problems.useAgain: when you need the size of a file and all you know is how many lines it has and how long a line is.
hints: Work out one line first, and remember the invisible character on the end of it.
Multiply your line size by the number of lines, then slide the answer up the zoom lever.
problems.socraticHint: How many kilobytes make a megabyte, and does knowing that change which option you pick?

variant.prompt: The generator writes a smaller case instead: 10,000 whole numbers, one per line, each up to three digits long. About how big is that file?

problems.prompt: Suppose the dawn log has been running one line a morning for nine weeks, and suppose about one morning a week got missed. About how many lines are in it?
explanation: Nine weeks of mornings is 9 times 7, which is 63.
About nine of those have no line, one for each week.
63 take away 9 leaves about 54, so about 55 lines. The gaps are part of the answer.
problems.useAgain: when you are asked how much data a real log holds and the log has gaps in it.
hints: Count the mornings that existed before you count the lines that got written.
Work out the whole nine weeks first, then take the misses off.
problems.socraticHint: If somebody asked you how many mornings the log covers, would that be the same number?

variant.prompt: Suppose the log ran for six weeks instead and about two mornings a week got missed. About how many lines are in it?

problem.prompt: On the driveway you chalk a straight line of 9 stones, one foot apart, and you have to stand on one of them. You want the total of your distances to all nine stones to be as small as it can be. What is that smallest total, in feet?
explanation: Try the middle stone, the fifth. The distances out from it are 4, 3, 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 feet, which add to 20.
Now shift one stone along, to the fourth. Five stones get further away and only four get closer, so the total climbs to 21.
Shifting the other way does the same thing.
So the best stone is the one with as many stones on one side as on the other, which is the median stone and not an average of anything.
problem.useAgain: when you have to pick a spot on a line that keeps the total distance to everything else small.
hints: Chalk it for real. Nine stones, stand on one of them, then add up the nine gaps.
Start on the middle stone and work out the total, then step one stone along and see which way the total moves.
problem.socraticHint: When you step one stone to the left, how many stones get closer and how many get further away?

variant.prompt: Now the line has 7 stones and they are two feet apart. You stand on one of them. What is the smallest possible total of your distances to all seven stones, in feet?

steps.title: The arc, measured: three middles, one spread, and the holes left in

problems.prompt: Seven dawn readings off the thermometer, in degrees: 60, 62, 63, 61, 64, 62, 41. The 41 was the morning a cold front came through. What is the mean?
explanation: Add all seven readings. They come to 413.
Seven mornings, so 413 divided by 7 is 59.
Now look at what that number does. Six of the seven mornings were 60 or warmer, and the mean sits below every one of them.
Mean, median and mode are three stories about one pile, and each of them can lie. Knowing which lies when is the skill.
problems.useAgain: when somebody hands you one number that is supposed to stand for a whole pile of numbers.
hints: Add before you divide, and put the 41 in the pile with the others.
Divide your total by how many mornings there were, not by how many were warm.
problems.socraticHint: Is the answer you got a temperature that any morning actually was?

variant.prompt: Seven readings from a different week: 70, 72, 71, 73, 72, 74, 51. What is the mean?

problems.prompt: Seven dawn readings off the thermometer, in degrees: 60, 62, 63, 61, 64, 62, 41. The 41 was the morning a cold front came through. What is the median?
explanation: Put them in order first: 41, 60, 61, 62, 62, 63, 64.
Seven readings means one sits dead centre with three on each side.
That is the fourth one along, which is 62.
Notice what the cold morning did. It moved to the front of the queue and changed nothing else.
problems.useAgain: when one strange reading is sitting in a pile and you want the typical one anyway.
hints: Sorting comes before anything else, and the odd reading gets sorted too.
With seven readings in order, count in from both ends until you meet.
problems.socraticHint: If the 41 had been a 4 instead, which of the mean and the median would move?

variant.prompt: Seven readings from a different week: 70, 72, 71, 73, 72, 74, 51. What is the median?

problems.prompt: Those seven dawn readings give a mean of 59, a median of 62, a mode of 62 and a range of 23. A grandparent on the phone asks what a typical dawn was like this week. Two of the four answers below carry the same number, so judge them by their reasons instead: which one is the right thing to tell her?
options: The mean, 59, because it uses every morning you wrote down.
The median, 62, because one strange morning cannot drag it far.
The mode, 62, because that reading turned up more often than any other.
The range, 23, because it says how spread out the week was.
explanation: The mean, 59, is not wrong, but no morning was 59 and six of the seven were warmer. One cold front dragged it there.
The median, 62, does not care how far out the odd morning was, only that it was one morning.
The mode is 62 here by luck. Change one reading so nothing repeats and the mode has nothing to say.
The range describes the spread, not a typical morning.
problems.useAgain: when you have to hand one number to somebody who will never see the whole list.
hints: Ask what the question wants: a typical morning, not a total and not a spread.
Check each of the four against the actual readings and see which one a morning could really have been.
problems.socraticHint: Which of these four would change most if that 41 had been a 51 instead?

variant.prompt: A practice log of minutes per problem: 21, 22, 23, 22, 24, 25, 45. That gives a mean of 26, a median of 23, a mode of 22 and a range of 24. Somebody asks how long a problem usually takes you. Which number answers that best?
options: The median, 23, because the one long problem cannot drag it.
The mean, 26, because it uses every problem you did.
The mode, 22, because that number turned up twice.
The range, 24, because it shows how spread out you are.

problems.prompt:
Aaliyah found the median of nine recorded practice times, in minutes: 14, 9, 11, 20, 10, 13, 12, 15, 16, like this:
Line 1: Put them in order: 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 20.
Line 2: Nine numbers means one sits in the exact middle, with four on each side.
Line 3: Counting in from the left, that is the fourth number, which is 12.
Line 4: So the median of these nine practice times is 12 minutes.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Line 3 is wrong: with four numbers on each side, the middle one is the fifth number along, not the fourth.
Lines 1 and 2 are both correct: the sort is right, and nine numbers really do put four on each side of the middle one.
The fifth number in the sorted list is 13, not 12, so the true median is 13 minutes.
Counting from the wrong end, or stopping one number short, easily lands on a neighbour of the median instead of the median itself.
problems.useAgain: when a sorted list has an odd number of entries and you need the exact middle one, not a neighbour of it.
hints: Count how many numbers sit on each side of the middle one before you decide which position that is.
For an odd-sized list, the middle position is one more than the count on either side.
problems.socraticHint: If there are four numbers before the middle one, what position number does the middle one itself have to be?

variant.prompt:
Aaliyah found the median of eight recorded practice times, in minutes: 9, 14, 11, 20, 10, 13, 12, 16, like this:
Line 1: Put them in order: 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 16, 20.
Line 2: Eight numbers means there is no single middle one, so the median is the average of the two middle numbers.
Line 3: The two middle numbers are the fourth and fifth: 12 and 13.
Line 4: The median is just the fourth number, 12, since it comes right before the split.
Which line is wrong?

problems.prompt: Recordings made in each of this season's first eight weeks: 2, 3, 2, 4, 3, 2, 3, 3. What is the mode?
explanation: The mode is the value that turns up most often, so tally rather than add.
2 turns up three times, 3 turns up four times, 4 turns up once.
So the mode is 3. It is not the biggest number here and not the middle one either.
problems.useAgain: when you want the most common value in a list rather than an average of it.
hints: Do not add these up. Count how many times each different number appears.
Make a small tally with one row per different value, then read off the tallest row.
problems.socraticHint: If every week had a different number of recordings, what would the mode be then?

variant.prompt: A different eight weeks: 5, 4, 5, 6, 4, 4, 5, 4. What is the mode?

problems.prompt: Suppose the dawn log covers 30 mornings but only 24 of the lines got filled in, because of travel and forgetting. Those 24 readings add up to 1,512. What is the mean of the readings you actually have?
explanation: Only 24 readings exist, so 24 is what you divide by. The 30 counts mornings, not readings.
1,512 divided by 24 is 63.
Then say what it is the mean of. This is a 24-morning mean, and you cannot make a 30-morning one out of it.
Real logs have holes, and an honest log names them instead of papering over them.
problems.useAgain: when a log you are working from is missing entries and somebody asks for a total or an average.
hints: Two numbers are offered here and only one of them counts readings.
Divide by how many readings you have got, then write down what your answer is actually the mean of.
problems.socraticHint: What would you have to assume about the six missing mornings to turn this into a 30-morning mean?

variant.prompt: Suppose a different log covers 28 mornings with 21 lines filled in, and those 21 readings add up to 1,428. What is the mean of the readings you actually have?

problems.prompt: The app's bug diary count says 19 for season 1 and 34 for season 3. Somebody reads that and says it proves you made more mistakes in season 3. True or false?
explanation: That count measures bugs you found and wrote down, not bugs that existed.
A season where you built more and looked harder shows a bigger number even if you were making fewer mistakes.
So the number is honest and it still does not answer the question asked of it. A count of work is not a score.
problems.useAgain: when somebody turns a count of work into a judgement about how good somebody is.
hints: Ask what the number was actually counting before you ask what it proves.
Think of two different reasons the count could go up, and see whether the claim can tell them apart.
problems.socraticHint: What would have to be true about your diary for that count to mean what they think it means?

variant.prompt: Somebody says that same 34 tells you how many bugs you found in season 3 rather than how many were in your programs. True or false?

steps.title: Cubes counted honestly, and twenty rolls compared to the math

problems.prompt: A storage box is 8 cm long, 5 cm wide and 4 cm tall. What is its volume, in cubic cm?
explanation: Volume fills the box with little cubes, edge times edge times edge.
8 times 5 times 4 is 160.
The unit has to be cubic cm, since three lengths were multiplied together, not two.
problems.useAgain: when a box's volume is found by multiplying all three of its edges, and the answer's unit has to be cubic, not square.
hints: Multiply all three edge lengths together, not just two of them.
Check the unit: three lengths multiplied gives a cubic unit.
problems.socraticHint: If area comes from multiplying two lengths, what does multiplying three lengths together give you instead?

variant.prompt: A storage box is 6 cm long, 5 cm wide and 3 cm tall. What is its volume, in cubic cm?

problems.prompt: That same 8 cm by 5 cm by 4 cm box has 6 faces. What is its total surface area, in square cm?
explanation: The box has 3 pairs of matching faces: 8 by 5, 8 by 4, and 5 by 4.
Those three face areas are 40, 32 and 20, adding to 92, then doubled for the matching pair of each.
92 times 2 is 184 square cm, a flat unit this time, not a cubic one.
problems.useAgain: when a box's total surface area is found from its net, adding the three pairs of matching faces.
hints: A box has three different face shapes, each appearing twice. Find each one's area.
Add all three, then double the total for the matching pair of each.
problems.socraticHint: Does surface area come from multiplying three edges together, or from adding up flat faces?

variant.prompt: That same 6 cm by 5 cm by 3 cm box's surface area, in square cm?

problems.prompt: A fair die is rolled 20 times and the results tallied: a 6 comes up 5 times. What fraction of the 20 rolls, in lowest terms, actually showed a 6?
explanation: The simulated fraction is just the tally count over the total rolls: 5 over 20.
5/20 simplifies to 1/4.
The calculated chance of a 6 is 1/6, so this short run of 20 rolls landed a bit above it.
problems.useAgain: when a real tally needs turning into a fraction, and then comparing to the calculated chance it is estimating.
hints: Write the tally count over the total number of rolls.
Simplify that fraction to lowest terms.
problems.socraticHint: Does a simulated fraction from just 20 rolls have to land exactly on the calculated probability?

variant.prompt: A fair die is rolled 20 times and a 6 comes up 3 times. What fraction of the 20 rolls, in lowest terms, showed a 6?

problems.prompt: A fair coin is flipped 20 times and heads comes up 11 times. What fraction of the 20 flips, in lowest terms, actually showed heads?
explanation: The simulated fraction is the heads count over the total flips: 11 over 20.
11/20 is already in lowest terms, since 11 shares no factor with 20.
The calculated chance of heads is 1/2, so this run landed close to it but not exactly on it.
problems.useAgain: when comparing a real coin-flip tally to the calculated 1 in 2 chance it is standing in for.
hints: Write the heads count over the total number of flips.
Check whether that fraction can be simplified further.
problems.socraticHint: Is landing close to, but not exactly on, the calculated chance a sign that something is wrong with the coin?

variant.prompt: A fair coin is flipped 20 times and heads comes up 8 times. What fraction of the 20 flips, in lowest terms, showed heads?

steps.title: The new tool: arrest the smallest criminal

problems.prompt: Suppose some claim about whole numbers turns out to be false for at least one whole number. Statement: then among all the whole numbers it is false for, there has to be a smallest one. True or false?
explanation: The numbers it fails on form a heap, and the heap is not empty, because you were told it fails somewhere.
Start at one failure and walk downwards. Every step down is a whole number, and whole numbers cannot fall forever.
So the walk stops, and where it stops is the smallest failure there is.
That is the new tool. Arrest the smallest criminal, squeeze a smaller accomplice out of it, and the crime never happened.
problems.useAgain: when you want to prove something is true for every whole number and you have no idea where to start.
hints: The claim fails somewhere. Ask whether it could keep failing further and further down forever.
Picture the failures as a pile of whole numbers and try to walk down through the pile.
problems.socraticHint: What is it about whole numbers, and not about all numbers, that makes the walk downwards stop?

variant.prompt: Suppose some claim about fractions between 0 and 1 turns out to be false for at least one of them. Statement: then among all the fractions it is false for, there has to be a smallest one. True or false?

problems.prompt: Here is the first case for the new tool. Claim: every whole number bigger than 1 is a product of primes, where a prime on its own counts as a product of one prime. Suppose the claim is false. Then there is a smallest criminal: call it N, the smallest whole number bigger than 1 that is not a product of primes. Arrest N. Write the argument that squeezes a smaller accomplice out of it and shows the crime never happened.

mustMention: N cannot be prime, because a prime already counts as a product of one prime
so N splits into a times b with both parts bigger than 1 and both smaller than N
a and b are smaller than N, so each of them is already a product of primes
putting those primes together writes N as a product of primes, so N was never a criminal

explanation: Ask what kind of number N could be. If N were prime it would already be a product of one prime, so N is not prime.
A number bigger than 1 that is not prime splits into a times b with both parts bigger than 1.
Both parts are smaller than N, and that is the accomplice.
N was the smallest criminal, so everything below N obeys the claim. So a and b are both products of primes.
Write a's primes beside b's primes and N is a product of primes after all.
No smallest criminal exists, and if there is no smallest one there is none at all.
problems.useAgain: when a claim about every whole number needs proving and breaking a number into smaller pieces is possible.
hints: Start by asking whether N could be prime, and say why that would end the argument immediately.
If N is not prime it splits into two parts. Ask how big those parts are compared with N.
problems.socraticHint: Where exactly in your argument do you use the fact that N was the smallest one, rather than just some criminal?

problems.prompt: A chocolate bar is a 4 by 6 grid of 24 squares. A break takes one piece and snaps it along a single straight line into two pieces. What is the smallest number of breaks that leaves all 24 squares separate?
explanation: Watch the number of pieces, not the chocolate. You start with one piece and you want 24.
Every break, wherever it is made, turns one piece into two, so the count goes up by exactly one.
Going from 1 to 24 takes 23 of those, and no order can beat it or lose to it.
The 4 and the 6 were the distraction. Only the 24 mattered.
problems.useAgain: when every move in a puzzle changes some count by the same amount and you need how many moves.
hints: Do not plan the breaks. Count something that every break changes in the same way.
How many pieces do you have before the first break, and how many after it?
problems.socraticHint: Is there any break you could make that adds two pieces at once?

variant.prompt: The bar is a 5 by 5 grid of 25 squares instead. What is the smallest number of breaks that leaves all 25 squares separate?

problems.prompt: A staircase lets you jump exactly 3 steps or exactly 5 steps at a time, as many jumps as you like in any order. What is the largest number of steps you cannot land on exactly?
explanation: List what you can reach: 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11 and onwards. The misses are 1, 2, 4 and 7.
So 7 is the biggest miss you can find by hand. Now show that nothing bigger is missed.
Land 8, 9 and 10 by hand first: 3 and 5, three 3s, two 5s. Now suppose N is the smallest miss above 7. Those three checks force N to be at least 11.

So N take away 3 is at least 8 and still smaller than N. Everything below N and at least 8 is reachable, because N is the smallest miss, so N take away 3 is reachable. One more jump of 3 lands on N. No smallest criminal, no criminal at all. Without the three checks N could be 10, and 10 take away 3 is 7, a miss.
problems.useAgain: when you have to show that everything past some point is reachable and the small cases are easy to check by hand.
hints: Start by listing which small numbers you can hit, in order, and mark the ones you cannot.
Once you find a run of reachable numbers, ask what one extra jump of 3 does to that run.
problems.socraticHint: If you can already reach some number, which other numbers does that hand you for free?

variant.prompt: The staircase now lets you jump exactly 4 steps or exactly 7 steps at a time. What is the largest number of steps you cannot land on exactly?

problems.prompt: AMC peak. A list of five positive whole numbers has a median of 3 and a mean of 11. What is the largest number that could be in the list?
explanation: Mean 11 across five numbers means they add to 55, and that total never moves.
Write them in order. The median is the third one, so the third is 3.
To make one huge, starve the rest. The first two are at least 1 each, and the fourth cannot be below the median, so at least 3.
That spends 8 of the 55, leaving 47. Check it: 1, 1, 3, 3, 47 has median 3 and mean 11.
problems.useAgain: when a mean and a median are both fixed and you are asked how extreme one entry can get.
hints: Turn the mean into a total straight away, because a total holds still while a mean does not.
Write the five in order and ask how small each of the other four is allowed to be.
problems.socraticHint: Why is the fourth number not allowed to be 1?

variant.prompt: A list of five positive whole numbers has a median of 4 and a mean of 10. What is the largest number that could be in the list?

problems.prompt: AMC peak. Six different whole numbers, each between 1 and 20, add up to 100. What is the smallest that the largest of the six could be?
explanation: Call the largest M. The other five are different and below M, so the greediest they can be is M-1 down to M-5.
Try M as 19: 19, 18, 17, 16, 15 and 14 add to 99, which is short of 100. So 19 cannot be the largest.
Try M as 20: 20, 19, 18, 17, 16 and 10 add to exactly 100.
Pushing on the largest and asking what the rest could possibly carry is the extremal move.
problems.useAgain: when a question asks for the smallest possible biggest thing, or the biggest possible smallest thing.
hints: Give the largest a name and ask how greedy the other five are allowed to be.
Test a candidate by making the other five as big as they are allowed to get, then compare the total with 100.
problems.socraticHint: If the six were allowed to repeat, would your answer change?

variant.prompt: Five different whole numbers, each between 1 and 20, add up to 80. What is the smallest that the largest of the five could be?

problems.prompt: Every whole number can be written as a sum of different powers of 2, with no power used twice. How many different powers of 2 does 100 need?
explanation: Take the biggest power of 2 that fits in 100. That is 64, and 36 is left.
Again: 32 fits in 36 and leaves 4, and 4 fits in 4 and leaves nothing. So 64 plus 32 plus 4, three powers.
The greedy step can never repeat a power, because the leftover is always smaller than the power you just took.
That shrinking leftover is the smallest criminal wearing a different coat.
problems.useAgain: when a number has to be built out of powers of 2 and you want to know it can always be done.
hints: Do not hunt for a clever combination. Take the biggest power of 2 that fits and look at what is left.
Write the powers of 2 in a row up to 128 first, then work down them.
problems.socraticHint: After you take the biggest power that fits, could the leftover ever be big enough to want that same power again?

variant.prompt: How many different powers of 2 does 90 need?

steps.title: The month 3 monster opens: the twelve coins
steps.body:
A monster is not a lesson. It goes on the home card, it stays there for the month, and it is yours to circle, poke and walk away from for days at a time. Nobody is going to teach you this one, and nobody is going to ask you for it this week.

Here it is, and it is the last monster of the four seasons.

Twelve coins sit on the table. Eleven of them are honest and weigh exactly the same. One is a fake. The fake is either heavier than an honest coin or lighter than an honest coin, and nobody has told you which. You have a two-pan balance and nothing else: no numbers, no weights, no scale to read. Each time you use it you learn one of three things, that the left pan went down, that the right pan went down, or that the two pans balanced.

You get three weighings. Find the fake coin, and say whether it is heavy or light.

Then the second half, which is the half that makes this a monster rather than a puzzle. Argue that three weighings are enough for twelve coins, and argue that two weighings could never be, however cleverly somebody chose them.

How to start, and it is the same advice as always. Make it smaller. Try three coins with a fake you have been told is heavy. Then four coins with the direction still unknown. Then nine. Watch what changes when the direction stops being known, because that is where the difficulty actually lives.

One thing worth asking early, and it is a question and not a hint. Before you weigh anything at all, how many different answers could this puzzle have? Count them properly, the heavy ones and the light ones both. Then ask how many different things a single weighing can tell you, and do not answer that one with a guess. Answer it by looking at the balance.

Build the balance itself if there is not one in the house. A coat hanger, two paper cups and two lengths of string will do it, and building it is part of the monster rather than a chore before it. Twelve coins of the same kind out of the coin jar, and one of them gets a pencil dot on the rim so you can play the fake yourself while somebody else solves it.

This one stays open on the home card. It gets performed for the family at the Grand Expedition, with real coins and the real balance, on the date the wall map gives it.

steps.title: Arrest the staircase, and write the arrest up
steps.prompt:
The staircase problem this morning asked for the largest number of steps you cannot land on with jumps of 3 and 5. Now prove the other half of it, in writing, to the rubric.

Claim: every number of steps from 8 upwards can be landed on exactly. Start by landing 8, 9 and 10 by hand and writing the jumps down, because everything after this stands on those three. Now suppose the claim is false and let N be the smallest number from 8 up that cannot be reached. Say why your three hand checks force N to be at least 11. Then say why N take away 3 is smaller than N and still at least 8, say what N being the smallest criminal tells you about that number, and say how one more jump of 3 finishes the arrest. Finish with one sentence on what would go wrong in the argument if you had skipped the three checks and started at 8 instead.

steps.title: Say the arrest out loud
steps.prompt: Two minutes, standing, no paper. Tell somebody who has never seen it how you know every whole number bigger than 1 is a product of primes. Name the smallest criminal, say what happens the moment you ask whether it is prime, and say where the smaller accomplice comes from. Then let your listener try to break it: ask them to offer any number they like as a criminal, and show them out loud what the argument does to it.
